unsupported: The whole family claim: ghost shrimp (Palaemonidae) in a separate family from cherry and Amano shrimp (Atyidae).
note: Searched for a taxonomic page placing Palaemonetes apart from Neocaridina and Caridina multidentata. The Smithsonian repository PDF (De Grave, Cai and Anker 2008) returned 403, and a second search found only hobby and retailer pages. Hobby pages also note that "ghost shrimp" is a loose trade name covering several species.

quote: For example, grit, needed by some passerines and Columbiformes (pigeons and doves) to aid in mechanical digestion of seeds ingested whole, is not needed by psittacines that remove seed hulls before ingestion.
unsupported: "upper beak has small ridges that hold a seed in place while the lower beak cracks and removes the hull" (the page says parrots remove hulls but not how the beak does it)
correctedFact: Parrotlets, like other parrots, strip the hull off a seed before they swallow it, and that is why they do not need grit. Pigeons, doves and some songbirds swallow seeds whole and need grit to grind them, but a parrot's seeds arrive already shelled.
note: The page covers psittacines as a group and does not name parrotlets.

quote: Males make clucking sounds during the mating process.
note: The page says "during the mating process" rather than courtship. The closing line about animals people assume are silent is framing, not a factual claim.

publisher: Los Angeles Zoo and Botanical Gardens
quote: The rosy boa is a mild-mannered snake. If hiding from a predator is not an option, it will try to confuse the adversary by making its tail appear to be its head. The boa will curl itself into a ball with its head in the center and wave its tail back and forth to look like a snake head ready to strike.
unsupported: "share their signature defensive move ... with the far larger ball python" (the page does not mention ball pythons); "rarely triggered at all" (the page says it balls up when hiding is not an option)
correctedFact: When a rosy boa feels threatened and cannot hide, it curls into a ball with its head tucked in the center. It then waves its tail back and forth so the tail looks like a head ready to strike, steering an attacker away from the parts that matter.

pageTitle: Dialect change in resident killer whales: implications for vocal learning and cultural transmission
quote: Resident killer whales live in stable social groups that are organized along maternal lines. The basic unit of their society is the matriline consisting of one to four generations of maternally related individuals. Dispersal of juveniles and adults from these groups appears to be absent in the resident communities (Bigg et al. 1990). ... Ford (1989, 1991) showed that groups of related matrilines called pods have unique vocal repertoires of 7–17 discrete call types ... [Ford] found that the dialects of resident killer whales are rather stable at the level of the vocal repertoire, since he detected no differences in the call types used by certain groups over a 30-year period.
unsupported: "led by a matriarch, the oldest female" (the paper describes maternal lines, not leadership); "clicks and whistles" (the dialects are discrete pulsed calls); "calves spend years learning" (the paper treats learning as likely but does not measure it)
correctedFact: Resident killer whales live in family groups built along the mother's line, and neither sons nor daughters have been seen leaving them. Each pod has its own set of calls, and one long study found no change in the call types some groups used over 30 years.
note: Applies to the resident orcas of the northeast Pacific, not all orcas. The paper itself found slow structural change in one call type over 12 to 13 years, so "nearly unchanged" holds for the repertoire, not every call.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: The female pushes leaves and branches into a nest pile where the eggs are incubated by the elevated temperatures of decomposition. The female remains on top of the nest to guard the eggs, and the male remains close by.
unsupported: "the only snake known to build a nest"; "spending days"; "compacting them into a waterproof mound"; "almost a meter tall"
correctedFact: A female king cobra builds a nest for her eggs. She pushes leaves and branches into a pile, lays her eggs inside, and the heat of the rotting leaves keeps them warm. She then stays on top of the nest to guard them, with the male close by.

quote: This fame partially stems from its practice of building and decorating a bower to attract females. This consists of two parallel walls of sticks, is built on the ground, and is used as a courtship arena during the breeding season. The male decorates it with bright blue coloured objects that it collects; blue clothes pegs, drinking straws and bottle tops are among the favourite stolen items ... The female places a loose nest of sticks in a tree or bush
unsupported: "even stealing blue items from rival bowers" (the page calls them stolen items without saying from where); "females favor males whose bowers are bluer"
correctedFact: A male satin bowerbird builds a bower to attract females, and it is not a nest: two parallel walls of sticks on the ground that serve as his courtship stage. He decorates it with bright blue objects, from parrot feathers and flowers to stolen bottle tops and drinking straws.

unsupported: The whole claim: temperature-sensitive pigment enzyme, kittens born nearly white, cooler extremities darkening.
note: Searched for the colorpoint mechanism. The UC Davis Veterinary Genetics Laboratory colorpoint page returned a Cloudflare block, and the CFA Siamese breed page says only that Siamese darken with age. A genetics paper on the cat tyrosinase gene would be the place to source it.

quote: Aardvarks have peg-like molars and premolars, but no incisors or canines ... Their teeth lack enamel and are made up of densely packed tubules, composed of a modified form of dentine. The tubules are contained in a sleeve of dental cement. ... The ants and termites are swept into their small mouth with their long, sticky tongue. ... The order to which aardvarks belong, Tubulidentata, is unique because it is the only mammalian order that is represented by a single species.
unsupported: "no roots"; "keep growing throughout life"; "hexagonal"; "unlike any other mammal's"; "roughly a foot long"; "by the thousands"
correctedFact: An aardvark's teeth are built differently from ours. They have no enamel at all. Instead each one is made of densely packed tiny tubes of a modified form of dentine, bundled together inside a sleeve of dental cement, and the animal has no front teeth or canines.
extraPoints: The aardvark is the only living species in its mammalian order, Tubulidentata.
At night it sweeps ants and termites into its mouth with a long, sticky tongue.

unsupported: The whole claim: blood squirting aimed at canids, the ant-derived chemical, squirt distance, and the weak effect on birds.
note: Searched for the Middendorf and Sherbrooke canid blood-squirting studies. The author page has been retired, the Texas Parks and Wildlife URL redirected to an unrelated page, and the BioOne abstract of the 2005 coyote study returned no text.

quote: The adult Bald Eagle plumage is unmistakable by 5.5 years, with the white head and tail contrasting the brown body. Young juveniles have a dark brown head, body, wings, and tail, with some whiteish mottling in wings and tail; older juveniles may have a whiter body.
unsupported: "and a dark bill"; "one of the most misidentified birds on the continent"; "almost always a young bald eagle rather than a golden eagle or some unplaceable hawk"
correctedFact: A young bald eagle looks nothing like the national emblem. Juveniles have a dark brown head, body, wings and tail with some whitish mottling, and older ones can show a whiter body. The clean white head and tail are not fully in place until about five and a half years of age.

quote: You might guess that its white head makes it look bald, but that’s not it! There is an old English word, “balde” which means white. We get the word “piebald” from this as well. Piebald means a mix of dark and white coloration, so it is easy to see why eagles would get a name relating to this word.
unsupported: "used of a horse or a bird marked in white patches" (the page defines piebald as a mix of dark and white coloration and names no animals)
correctedFact: The bald eagle has a full head of feathers. Its name comes from balde, an old English word meaning white, so the bird is really the white-headed eagle. The same word survives in piebald, which describes anything marked in a mix of dark and white.
note: The source is a science center blog post. Etymonline and other dictionaries were blocked to fetch, so the owner may want a dictionary source for the etymology.

pageTitle: 7 Things You Didn't Know About the Norwegian Lundehund
quote: The Lundehund has six fully developed toes on each foot. Four point forward and two point inward, like a human thumb. The extra toes provide more traction and grip when the dog is navigating the steep or slippery rocks and peaks of his Norwegian homeland. ... he is capable of touching the top of his head to his back, which enables him to turn around while inside a narrow underground passageway. The Lundehund also has an extremely flexible shoulder joint, allowing him to spread his forelegs out to the sides.
unsupported: "extra joints in its shoulders" (the page says an extremely flexible shoulder joint); "neck vertebrae" (the page describes the bend, not the vertebrae)
correctedFact: The Norwegian Lundehund has six fully developed toes on each foot, an extremely flexible shoulder joint, and a neck that lets it touch the top of its head to its back. Each trait is a puffin hunting tool, giving grip on steep, slippery rock and room to turn around inside narrow passages.

pageTitle: Dancing for Food in the Deep Sea: Bacterial Farming by a New Species of Yeti Crab
quote: a new species of Yeti crab, which we describe as Kiwa puravida n. sp, farms the epibiotic bacteria that it grows on its chelipeds (claws), chelipeds that the crab waves in fluid escaping from a deep-sea methane seep. Lipid and isotope analyses provide evidence that epibiotic bacteria are the crab's main food source and K. puravida n. sp. has highly-modified setae (hairs) on its 3 rd maxilliped (a mouth appendage) which it uses to harvest these bacteria. ... We hypothesize that this species waves its arm in reducing fluid to increase the productivity of its epibionts by removing boundary layers which may otherwise limit carbon fixation. ... In 2005 a new family of crab was discovered at a hydrothermal vent. This crab had chelipeds (claws) covered in dense setae and epibiotic bacteria
unsupported: "where there is nothing else to eat"; the waving is stated as fact, but the paper offers it as a hypothesis
correctedFact: The yeti crab Kiwa puravida farms its own food. Bacteria grow on the dense bristles of its claws, and the crab harvests them with comb-like mouthparts. Researchers think its constant claw waving keeps fresh seep water flowing past the bacteria so they keep growing.

pageTitle: Marine iguanas: the incredible shrinking lizards of the Galápagos
quote: Galápagos marine iguanas are the only lizards known to forage for food in the ocean. ... To cope with the amount of salt they consume while grazing in the ocean, marine iguanas have a specially adapted gland that removes salt from their bodies. They then forcefully expel the salt out of their nostrils in a sneeze-like fashion.
unsupported: "cannot process it through the kidneys alone"; "a gland above each eye"; "straight out of the bloodstream"; "a white crust dried across the snout and the top of the head"
correctedFact: The marine iguana is the only lizard known to forage in the ocean, grazing algae off submerged rocks. All that seawater brings in a lot of salt, so a specially adapted gland pulls it out of the body, and the iguana blasts it out through its nostrils in a sneeze.
note: Galapagos Conservancy pages tried first returned 404.

publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2005)
pageTitle: Bite club: comparative bite force in big biting mammals and the prediction of predatory behaviour in fossil taxa
quote: Estimated BS adjusted for body mass was higher for marsupials than placentals and the Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii) had the highest relative BS among extant taxa.
unsupported: "of any living mammal" (the ranking covers the living predators in the study sample); "higher than lions or tigers" (not named in the abstract); "crunch through entire carcasses, bones, fur and all"; "wears their teeth down to blunt nubs over a lifetime"
correctedFact: For its size, the Tasmanian devil had the strongest bite of any living predator in a landmark study of mammal bite force. Researchers compared bite force against body mass across living and fossil meat eaters, and the devil came out on top among the living species.
note: Only the abstract could be read; the full text was not retrievable.

quote: Algae may cover much of the carapace causing the animal to virtually disappear into its surroundings. ... The mandibles are not attached medially, and the relatively weak jaws are unsuited for seizing and chewing prey. ... When a potential prey item comes within range of the turtle, the turtle will strike out and open its mouth. Large amounts of water, and the prey item, are sucked in by the low pressure that is created. The mouth is then closed and excess water is expelled. The prey item is swallowed whole.
unsupported: "bark-like skin flaps make it nearly invisible" (the page credits algae on the shell for the camouflage and says the flaps' function is uncertain); "on a muddy riverbed"
correctedFact: The matamata's jaws are too weak to grab or chew prey. Instead, when a fish swims close, the turtle strikes and throws its mouth open, and the low pressure sucks in water and fish together. It shuts its mouth, pushes the water back out and swallows the fish whole.

publisher: The University of the West Indies
pageTitle: Nyctibius griseus (Common Potoo), The Online Guide to the Animals of Trinidad and Tobago
quote: the adult adopts the characteristic feature of a stump or dead wood. It does this by having a still posture where its head would be raised and the bill, the neck would be outstretched and the plumage would be compressed ... Potoos have unsual slits in the eye lids which allow them to sense movement when eyes are closed (Borrero, 1974).
unsupported: the "poor me one" call; "by day" (the page describes the pose as a response to disturbance)
correctedFact: A common potoo hides by holding perfectly still with its head and bill raised, posing as a stump or piece of dead wood. Even with its eyes shut it is not blind to danger: unusual slits in its eyelids let it sense movement while it looks fast asleep.
note: The original eyelid study (Borrero 1974, The Condor) now redirects away from the SORA archive.

pageTitle: An Introduction to the Shiba Inu (part 2)
quote: He may pull back and scream a little, but that is natural. Encouragement and praise help, and soon he will be walking with you. ... A Shiba could go his whole life without every experiencing a brush, comb or bath and be just as healthy and happy. Shibas have little odor to their fur unless they have rolled in something pungent.
unsupported: "famous for the Shiba scream, a piercing, high-pitched shriek"; "during nail trims, baths, or vet visits" (the page mentions screaming only during leash training); "grooms itself like a cat, licking its paws and coat clean"
correctedFact: Shiba Inus are not shy about protesting. The National Shiba Club of America notes that a puppy meeting the leash for the first time may pull back and scream a little, and says this is natural: with encouragement and praise, the puppy is soon walking along with you.
extraPoints: Shibas groom themselves like cats and have little doggy odor.
note: The AKC breed page returned almost no text. The scream as a named breed trait could not be confirmed on a club or kennel page; the owner may prefer to rebuild this card around the low-odor point, which the club page does support.

publisher: Los Angeles Zoo and Botanical Gardens
quote: The serval’s success lies in a sound-hunting technique that targets prey with great precision. The cat’s large ears rotate like radar dishes, and ultrasonic hearing allows them to tune into the high-pitched sounds that rodents produce, even underground.
unsupported: "the largest ears of any cat for their body size" (not on this page); "each ear can swivel on its own" (the page says the ears rotate, not independently); "calls rodents use to talk to each other" (the page says high-pitched sounds rodents produce); "hidden in tall grass" (the page says even underground)
correctedFact: A serval hunts by sound. Its large ears rotate like radar dishes, and its hearing reaches into the ultrasonic range, so it can tune in to the high-pitched sounds rodents make, even when the prey is underground. It is a big part of why servals catch prey on about half their attempts.
note: The San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance serval fact sheet, read first, has a caption saying servals have the largest ears of any cat but does not cover ultrasonic hearing.

publisher: Los Angeles Zoo and Botanical Gardens
quote: Servals will use their long limbs to reach into burrows, catching mice, rats, or shrews with their sharp claws. ... Long legs and a long neck allow them to peer over tall grasses.
unsupported: "the longest legs for its body size of any cat" (not on this page)
correctedFact: A serval's long legs do more than lift its head above tall grass. When a mouse, rat or shrew is hiding in a burrow, the serval reaches a long leg down the hole and catches the prey with its sharp claws.
note: The San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance serval fact sheet, read first, lists "Longest legs (relative to body size) of any other cat species" but does not mention reaching into burrows.

quote: A sea otter may hunt on the seafloor but always returns to the surface to eat. Floating there on its back, it uses its chest as a table. ... An otter's coat has pockets—loose skin under each forearm. An otter uses them to stash prey during a dive, which leaves its paws free to hunt some more.

unsupported: The whole claim: foul-smelling secretion coated on eggs, chicks aiming droppings at intruders, and the rotting meat smell.
note: Searched for the hoopoe nest defense. The Soler et al. 2008 Functional Ecology PDF at the University of Granada repository was blocked, and the one paper reached (Journal of Experimental Biology 2009, "Symbiotic bacteria living in the hoopoe's uropygial gland prevent feather degradation", abstract only) covers gland bacteria that protect feathers, not smell, egg coating or droppings.

quote: All Manx cats are heterozygous for the Manx gene (i.e. Mm), which means they have one mutant M gene and one normal m gene. The mutant M gene is dominant to the normal m gene (Long 2006). Homozygous MM cats with two mutant genes are so abnormal they die early during foetal development, thus the Manx gene is described as a lethal gene (Long 2006). ... The mutant M gene has variable expression and so individuals have variable degrees of tail-lessness.
unsupported: "which is why responsible breeders never pair two tailless Manx cats together" (the page gives no breeding advice; it says completely tailless rumpy cats are most often affected by spina bifida); "shorten the spine itself" (the page says the gene disrupts the tail and sacral vertebrae and the spinal cord)
correctedFact: Manx cats carry one copy of a dominant gene that disrupts the tail bones, and it shows up to different degrees, from no tail at all to a nearly full one. The same gene can damage the spine near the hips, and a kitten with two copies dies early in development.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: Genetic studies show that it is neither fox nor true wolf, but a distinct species. It is the only member of its genus, Chrysocyon. ... Maned wolves are omnivorous eaters and primarily solitary hunters. They eat seasonally abundant fruits and vegetables and are particularly interested in lobeira, whose name means "fruit of the wolf." It is a small tomato-like berry that, along with other fruits and vegetables, makes up 50 percent of the maned wolf's diet. ... Crepuscular to nocturnal. Social Structure Maned wolves live in monogamous pairs sharing a 10 square mile (26 square kilometer) territory.
unsupported: "raise pups together" (the page says females raise the pups, with evidence that males bring them food)
correctedFact: The maned wolf is neither a wolf nor a fox but the only member of its own genus. About half of what it eats is fruit and vegetables, led by a small tomato-like berry called lobeira. Mated pairs share a territory, yet each one hunts alone, mostly at dusk and through the night.

pageTitle: Oscillation of the velvet worm slime jet by passive hydrodynamic instability
quote: The rapid squirt of a proteinaceous slime jet endows velvet worms (Onychophora) with a unique mechanism for defence from predators and for capturing prey by entangling them in a disordered web that immobilizes their target. ... In this case the maximum shooting distance was 0.54 m.
unsupported: "up to a foot away" (the longest squirt filmed in the study reached 0.54 m, about 21 inches); "hardening in seconds"; "basic body plan has barely changed in hundreds of millions of years"; "one of the closest things alive to a true living fossil"
correctedFact: A velvet worm hunts with slime. It squirts a fast jet of protein slime from fleshy nozzles beside its mouth, and the jet whips back and forth as it flies, tangling prey in a messy web that pins it in place. The longest squirt filmed in one study reached about 21 inches.
extraPoints: Velvet worms are living fossils whose body plan has barely changed in hundreds of millions of years.

publisher: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance Library
quote: Camouflage themselves by stretching head and body into straight line, tightening feathers against body, closing eyes, and freezing in place; resemble a tree branch. ... Daytime roosting behavior includes sitting in a relaxed or camouflaged posture (if disturbed), presumably to avoid detection by daytime avian predators
unsupported: "called stumping"; "eyes narrowed to slits" (the page says closing eyes); "snapped off" (the page says a tree branch)
correctedFact: When a tawny frogmouth wants to vanish, it stretches its head and body into one straight line, pulls its feathers tight, closes its eyes and freezes. Perched like that it looks like part of the tree, a branch rather than a bird, which helps it avoid daytime predators.
